Name: Non-Equivalent Data Transformation
Description:
The product parses or transforms data into another format,
	    structure, or representation, but the newly-produced data
	    is not semantically equivalent to the original data.

CommonConsequences.Note: The consequences vary depending on how the transformed data is intended to be used. If the data influences behavior of the product such as affecting how a security decision is made, then this could bypass an intended protection mechanism.

Entries.IntroText: Consider a product that uses an automated language translation service that is used to translate vendor-controlled web pages that are used for technical support. Consider that these web pages include domain names and email addresses for users to access.

Entries.ExampleCode: The product invokes the translation service on the entire message text without any special treatment or consideration for contact information such as email addresses and domain.

Entries.BodyText: If the translation is from English to Polish, then "example.com" might be translated to "przyklad.com" - a different web site entirely. Alternately, an email address such as "address@example.com" could be translated to "adres@przyklad.com". If an attacker can control the domain or email address that is generated by the translation, then the attacker might be able to spoof communications with the product's users.

Entries.ExampleCode: The code could be changed to mark which words or phrase should not be translated. Alternately, the original web pages could be structured in a way that uses templates that insert non-translatable data such as email addresses. A third option could be to analyze the resulting output and compare expected data elements against an allowlist of known-valid values.

ObservedExamples.Description: Web Application Firewall (WAF) does not parse HTTP multipart requests correctly, allowing bypass.
JavaScript URL library does not correctly parse URLs with leading whitespace.

DetectionMethods.Description: Examine inputs that will be saved or otherwise processed, then look at how they are produced in output. Analyze outputs that are expected to be (1) unchanged from the inputs, or (2) changed in a controlled way. Consider analyzing the data to extract key elements, such as e-mail addresses or domain names, to ensure that they are consistent with the original input.
DetectionMethods.EffectivenessNotes: These methods could have mixed results depending on how the product receives the data, transforms it, and outputs the data. It might require domain-specific knowledge of the product's intended behavior in order to determine if some transformations were correct. These methods could be time-consuming and not necessarily complete, but there might not be well-established and well-understood methods for some subtypes of this weakness.

PotentialMitigations.Description: Validate the transformed data against what was expected to be produced. If the data is complex and free-form with some "special elements" in them, consider re-parsing the output to ensure that it matches expectations.
